title: An All-van-der-Waals Qubit
authors: Sein Park, Sameia Zaman, Junghyun Kim, Junyoung An, Daniel Rodan-Legrain, Hung-Yu Tsao, Chia-Chin Tsai, Aranya Goswami, Réouven Assouly, William P. Banner, Gabriel D. Cutter, Kenji Watanabe, Takashi Taniguchi, Terry P. Orlando, Gil-Ho Lee, Kyle Serniak, Max Hays, Jeffrey A. Grover, Philip Kim, Pablo Jarillo-Herrero, Joel Î-j. Wang, William D. Oliver
abstract: Advances in solid-state physics, materials science, and device engineering have accelerated the development of superconducting qubits. Among emerging platforms, van der Waals (vdW) materials and their heterostructures are potentially attractive building blocks for quantum devices, yet their realization in qubit architectures remains largely underexplored. Here we report an all-vdW superconducting qubit based on a NbSe$_2$-hBN-NbSe$_2$ junction, in which a thin hBN layer simultaneously provides Josephson coupling and capacitive shunting between two NbSe$_2$ islands, forming a "merged-element" transmon. Temporal characterization using circuit quantum electrodynamics (cQED) techniques yields an average energy-relaxation time $T_{1,\mathrm{avg}} = 55 ~μs$, Hahn-echo coherence time $T_{2\mathrm{E},\mathrm{avg}} = 21 ~μs$, and Ramsey coherence time $T_{2\mathrm{R},\mathrm{avg}} = 1.9~μs$. The relatively low Ramsey time is primarily attributable to an enhanced sensitivity to charge noise consistent with the realized device parameters and not a fundamental limitation. These results show that lumped-element superconducting qubits based on vdW heterostructures can achieve coherence times comparable to those of conventional Al-AlO$_\mathrm{x}$-Al qubits, while offering a reduced device footprint and suppressed stray capacitive coupling.
summary: This paper reports on the realization and characterization of an all-van-der-Waals superconducting qubit using a NbSe2-hBN-NbSe2 junction. By employing cQED techniques, the authors measured coherence times comparable to established superconducting qubits. The work is significant because it proves that vdW heterostructures can form compact, high-performance qubits for quantum information processing.
main_problem: The primary goal is to develop superconducting qubits using van der Waals (vdW) materials to create compact, low-loss, and scalable quantum devices.
main_result: The all-vdW qubit achieved coherence times comparable to conventional Al-AlOx-Al qubits while offering a reduced device footprint due to the merged-element geometry.
method: The study employed circuit quantum electrodynamics (cQED) techniques, including spectroscopy, Rabi oscillations, and Ramsey/Hahn-echo measurements, to characterize the qubit performance.
model_or_system: The system is an all-vdW superconducting qubit based on a NbSe2-hBN-NbSe2 junction, modeled using the Cooper-pair-box Hamiltonian. The hBN layer acts as both the Josephson coupler and the shunt capacitor.
key_observables: Average energy-relaxation time ($T_{1,\mathrm{avg}} = 55 \mu	ext{s}$), Hahn-echo coherence time ($T_{2\mathrm{E},\mathrm{avg}} = 21 \mu	ext{s}$), and Ramsey coherence time ($T_{2\mathrm{R},\mathrm{avg}} = 1.9 \mu	ext{s}$).
important_parameters: Josephson energy ($E_J/h = 4.29 	ext{ GHz}$), Charging energy ($E_C/h = 0.13 	ext{ GHz}$), and the ratio $E_J/E_C \approx 33$.
main_assumptions: The relatively low Ramsey time is attributed to enhanced sensitivity to charge noise rather than being a fundamental limitation of the platform.
figures_summary: Figure 1 details the fabrication process and circuit layout. Figure 2 presents spectroscopy and Rabi oscillation measurements used for characterization.
paper_structure: The paper details the fabrication of the all-vdW qubit, characterizes its superconducting parameters using cQED techniques, measures key coherence times ($T_1, T_2$), and analyzes the sources of dephasing limitations.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the hardware challenge in quantum computing by demonstrating a viable, scalable material platform (vdW heterostructures) for superconducting qubits, which is highly relevant to open quantum systems research.
